newsitem.title: USA: U.S. certifies Mexico as anti-drugs ally.
newsitem.headline: U.S. certifies Mexico as anti-drugs ally.

text.p: The United States announced on Friday it was again certifying Mexico as an ally in the war on drugs, averting a potential diplomatic crisis with its neighbour but fuelling a domestic political controversy.

"President Bill Clinton has ... decided to grant Mexico a full certification but with firm expectations of further progress (in its fight against drugs) in the near term," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said in announcing certification decisions for 32 countries.
"We expect Mexico to work with us to meet a series of objectives that have emerged from our cooperation in the past."

The announcement -- tensely awaited in Mexico City and other capitals -- was part of an annual process in which the United States "certifies" whether other countries that are sources or way-stations for international narcotics trafficking are helping in the war against drugs.
Failure to be certified can lead to harsh U.S. economic and trade sanctions, as well as a diplomatic black eye.

Albright said 23 countries including Mexico had been certified as U.S. drug-fighting allies, six including Colombia had been denied certification and three -- Belize, Lebanon and Pakistan -- had been denied certification but given "national security waivers" sparing them U.S. economic punishments that may accompany decertification.
The decision on Colombia also stirred intense interest.

"This year, like last year, the president's decision to deny certification to Colombia was the result of our concern that corruption remains rampant at the highest levels of the Colombian government and that senior officials are failing to ... cooperate with us in the fight against drugs," Albright said.
"In no way is it meant to undercut the valiant and effective efforts of those Colombians who are fighting on the front lines against the drug trade."
The United States accuses Colombian President Ernesto Samper of taking millions of dollars in bribes from drug-traffickers to finance his 1994 election campaign.

Mexico's certification status had come into serious question in the past few days with the announcement of corruption charges against the official leading its anti-drugs efforts, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo. He has been arrested and charged with taking bribes from drug kingpins.
That has sparked calls in Congress to decertify Mexico as corrupt and untrustworthy as a U.S. partner in the drug war.

As word of Clinton's decision circulated through the U.S. capital, Democratic Sen. Dianne Feinstein of California, which borders Mexico, said she would lead an effort to have Congress disapprove Clinton's Mexico certification decision.
White House officials indicated in advance they expected such political backlash but the president was determined to proceed in what he felt was the country's best interests.

Mexico is the United States' third-largest trading partner, and its economic health is of prime concern to Washington. In addition, the two countries share a 2,000-mile (3,200 kms) border with Mexico, making Mexico's cooperation in the drugs war essential.

Mexican officials have expressed annoyance at the need to be "graded" by Washington on their efforts and Foreign Affairs Minister Jose Angel Gurria had suggested decertification could fracture bilateral relations between the two countries.
Albright said Washington gave Mexico high marks for the strides it had made to date in fighting drug-traffickers and had high requirements for further progress.
Assistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard said support for continuing certification for Mexico was unanimous among U.S. government agencies.
